That hearing is just one on the congressional calendar.

Huang and Nvidia's top lawyer have also agreed to appear in a closed-door hearing before a trio of House committees.

That joint effort by the House's Foreign Affairs, Intelligence, and China Select committees is set to meet behind closed doors with Huang on Dec. 1. Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter will then appear in another closed hearing on Dec. 2.

"We look forward to hearing from Jensen Huang and Tim Teter on their roles in a potential breach of our national security," Republican Reps. Brian Mast of Florida, John Moolenaar of Michigan, and Rick Crawford of Arkansas said in a joint statement , adding that both interviews will be transcribed.

articles.title: Hourly workers are living with 7.86% inflation. No wonder they voted against the AI boom
articles.summary: The backlash and the buildout are one problem.
articles.body:
On Nov. 3, in 40 of 41 local votes across 10 states, Americans chose to limit data centers. Many observers read that as voters choosing a recession over the biggest industrial buildout of their lifetimes .

I read it differently. Hourly workers are short on paycheck, and the warehouses near those data centers are short on hourly workers. The backlash and the buildout are one problem seen from two ends.

I see both ends because my company staffs those warehouses, which also means a tight labor market is good for our business. The figures below come from our shift and survey data unless I note otherwise.

Headline inflation was 3.7% in September . The Bureau of Labor Statistics itself says the CPI " does not necessarily measure your own experience with price change ." For hourly workers, the gap is wide. In our survey of 3,083 hourly workers this summer , 69.4% said they earn under $30,000 a year across all their jobs, and only about half have a savings account.

So I rebuilt the number around how these workers spend. I call it FeelFlation. We took each category's share of take-home pay and weighted it by how much that category's cost rose in the 12 months through September (figures rounded):

Rent or mortgage: 28% of take-home pay, costs up 3%

The weighted total is 7.86%, more than double the headline. The interest increase is our estimate from Consumer Financial Protection Bureau data, combining higher interest rates with balances that stay unpaid longer. If anything, 7.86% understates the squeeze, since newer data put insurance premiums up 16%.

Three categories do most of the damage: interest, insurance premiums and transportation. Together they take 41% of the paycheck and drive nearly 80% of the increase. Interest alone adds more than three points, and it's a cost the official gauge leaves out. The CPI tracks the prices of what people buy and excludes the interest on the credit cards and auto loans they use to pay for it. Gas prices make people angry because they see them every day. A debt bill that eats one dollar in six does more damage, quietly.

Hourly pay on our platform rose 3.1% over the same 12 months. The things these workers pay for rose 4.76 percentage points faster than their pay, and they're responding the only way they can. In that same survey , 67.6% said they pick up an extra shift rather than borrow when an unexpected bill hits.

articles.title: Elon Musk’s Giving Went Mostly to His Own Charity Last Year
articles.summary: Elon Musk’s foundation gave away nearly $400 million in 2025, more than three-quarters of which went to another nonprofit of his, according to the organizati...
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- Elon Musk's foundation gave away nearly $400 million in 2025, more than three-quarters of which went to another nonprofit of his, according to the organization's most recent tax filing.

The Musk Foundation sent more than $310 million in 2025 to The Foundation, a nonprofit he set up in 2023 to create a STEM-focused school and, eventually, a university, the filing shows. Another $20 million went to a donor-advised fund at Fidelity Charitable, which Musk also has control over. DAFs are a philanthropic tool that allow contributors to get the tax break associated with charitable activity before making donations to actual working charities.

Other gifts from Musk last year went to organizations based in the Memphis area, where the artificial intelligence arm of SpaceX has data centers. Slingshot Memphis received $5.9 million to "support poverty-fighting organizations," and $9.4 million went to the city's Regional One Health Foundation for "patient care needs."

Meanwhile, the Musk Foundation added more than $1 billion in assets, including a gift of $64 million in Tesla shares, for a total of about $16 billion.

Musk's fortune has more than doubled over the past year to $893 billion, according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index. In June, he became the world's first trillionaire — a title he's held on and off as the value of his companies fluctuates.

Musk, 55, is the chief executive officer of Tesla Inc. and SpaceX, which are both worth more than $1 trillion. Boards at each company have formed special committees to discuss a potential merger, Musk said in October.

In 2012, Musk signed the Giving Pledge, a promise to donate the majority of his wealth during his lifetime or in his will. However, his giving has failed to keep pace with the rapid growth of his fortune: He disclosed giving away roughly $1.4 billion from 2021 to 2024 even as his net worth grew by hundreds of billions of dollars.

This year marked the second-straight election cycle in which Musk was the country's biggest political donor, spending nearly half a billion dollars on a number of Republican candidates. His efforts largely failed. Democrats won all seven of the competitive Senate races he backed and all but two of the roughly 40 House races.

articles.title: 'Sending a message': Nvidia signals more cautious stance on China after Huang's departure
articles.summary: Nvidia's decision to halt Hopper chip sales to China may signal a more cautious shift on US-China relations from the leading chipmaker.
articles.body:
In the wake of Jensen Huang's meteoric fall from grace at Nvidia, the embattled company appears to be growing more cautious about China as new export controls and increasingly fractious state politics further complicate the AI footrace between Washington and Beijing.

Interim CEO Colette Kress said on Tuesday that while Nvidia booked $2.4 billion in revenue from sales of the company's "Hopper" chips to China in its fiscal third quarter, the company has halted shipments of those chips to Chinese firms and is modeling no revenue from those sales going forward.

The announcement marks a major shift for the company, which under Huang's leadership had aggressively pursued license from the Trump administration to sell its products into the world's second-largest economy.

The Commerce Department initially implemented sweeping restrictions on Nvidia's ability to sell its advanced semiconductors in China in 2022 under the Biden administration, largely closing the Chinese market to Huang's company. The Trump administration loosened those restrictions in 2025 amid US-China trade talks, approving Nvidia to export H200 chips — now three generations behind the company's leading products — to China.

Sales of those chips to China have accounted for only a small fraction of Nvidia's data center revenue, comprising less than 1% of data center sales in its fiscal second quarter and roughly 2.2% in its fiscal third quarter. That's partially due to Beijing slow-walking import approvals of the chips as Xi Jinping pushes for Chinese firms to build on domestic hardware, reducing their dependence on the American market.

Yet Huang himself has for years insisted that the US should further open Nvidia's access to China, arguing that by restricting Chinese access to American chips and foregoing potential Chinese dependence on US technology, Washington is only encouraging China to accelerate its own technological progress.

"Local companies are very talented, and the export controls gave them the spirit and energy to accelerate their development," Huang said in 2025 at a conference in Taipei , per local reporting. He repeated the sentiment in October 2026, telling Bloomberg , "I think we [the US] made a mistake, and this mistake is hard to unwind."

Public reporting and government investigations have revealed a shadow trade for the company's most advanced chips that has developed despite the US export regime. Accounts on Douyin, the nation's version of TikTok, openly offer sanctioned chips such as Nvidia's Blackwell B300 to buyers in videos reviewed by Yahoo Finance.

articles.title: Fed’s Waller says officials may need to ‘shock’ with half-point rate hike
articles.summary: Christopher Waller, a member of the Federal Reserve board of governors, said on Wednesday that central bank officials may need to “shock people” at their next meeting in early December, indicating he may back a half-point interest rate hike. During an interview with CNBC’s Steve Liesman, Waller said he is “very concerned” about inflation, which…
articles.body:
Christopher Waller, a member of the Federal Reserve board of governors, said on Wednesday that central bank officials may need to “shock people” at their next meeting in early December, indicating he may back a half-point interest rate hike .

During an interview with CNBC’s Steve Liesman, Waller said he is “very concerned” about inflation , which is “headed in the wrong direction” and “spreading out” beyond energy prices .

Given that, Waller said the Fed should “start taking more aggressive actions” in its monetary policy approach .

Officials on the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) raised rates by a quarter point in September amid persistent inflation, the first rate hike since July 2023 . The FOMC held rates steady at a range of 3.75 percent to 4 percent last month.

Traders are pricing in a 92.7 percent chance of officials raising rates by another quarter point at their Dec. 8-9 meeting, according to the CME FedWatch tool .

But Waller, whom President Trump nominated to the board during his first term , said businesses passing on elevated costs to consumers leads him to believe more aggressive Fed action is necessary.

“You might need to … shock people to say, ‘Wait a minute, 3 percent is not the number you should be thinking about going forward,’” he told Liesman.

Annual inflation has remained above the Fed’s 2 percent target for five and a half years and is up relative to before the Iran war .

The conflict , which is approaching the nine-month mark , led to a spike in energy prices in the U.S. due to the Islamic Republic’s restrictions on shipping in the Strait of Hormuz.

The Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA) will release data next Wednesday from the personal consumption expenditures (PCE) price index, the Fed’s preferred inflation metric.

Gas prices have declined recently, in line with seasonal trends, but remain above pre-war levels.

In September, annual PCE inflation was 3.6 percent . Without including more volatile food and energy costs, prices were up 3.1 percent from September 2025, the BEA reported .

Fed Chair Kevin Warsh has consistently stressed his goal of lowering inflation down to 2 percent since he took over at the central bank in May.

“We will deliver price stability — no ifs, ands, or buts. And that continues to be the case,” Warsh told reporters last month, after officials held rates steady.

articles.title: US lawmakers launch probe into Lutnick’s actions amid Nvidia scandal
articles.summary: Letter alleges possible conflict of interest in commerce secretary not adding Megaspeed to US trade blacklist.
articles.body:
Democratic lawmakers have opened a probe into whether United States Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick used his position to help Cantor Fitzgerald, an investment firm controlled by his two sons, avoid financial losses amid the scandal involving Jensen Huang at artificial intelligence chip giant Nvidia.

In the five-page letter dated November 17, House Democrats notified Brandon Lutnick, chairman of Cantor Fitzgerald and Howard Lutnick’s son, that they are requesting information to ascertain whether “any actions or decisions by Secretary Lutnick concerning export controls, enforcement measures, or national security policies may have been improperly influenced by Cantor Fitzgerald’s holdings or business interests”.

The letter was authored by Jamie Raskin of Maryland, who is the ranking member of the House Judiciary Committee, Gregory Meeks of New York and the ranking member of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, and Sydney Kamlager-Dove of California. It asks if the company’s financial exposure influenced Lutnick’s decision to keep Megaspeed off the US Entity List, a trade blacklist.

Megaspeed is attached to Alice Huang, the alleged Chinese spy who reportedly had an affair with now-former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who resigned last week.

The US adds companies to the Entity List if it determines they pose a risk to US national security or foreign policy.

“The Secretary has fully complied with the terms of his ethics agreement, including all divestiture and recusal requirements, and will continue to do so. He has divested all financial interests in Cantor Fitzgerald, Newmark, and BGC,” a Commerce Department spokesperson said in a statement in response to the letter, which was first reported by the Financial Times.

Cantor Fitzgerald denied the claims in the letter, saying it holds no material proprietary position in Nvidia. Cantor’s Nvidia holdings arise primarily from equity swaps executed for clients, according to the Reuters news agency.

The firm also said it has no role in US export control or Entity List decisions.

Earlier this month, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said four government agencies had favoured putting Megaspeed on a trade blacklist, but the Commerce Department, which was in charge, had not.

Reuters also reported that senior White House officials have discussed whether Lutnick should be pushed out.

On Tuesday, Huang, in his first public statement after he stepped down from Nvidia, said he would be “honored” to return as CEO, but the company’s board during its earnings call later in the day ruled out bringing him back.

articles.title: Tech layoffs flare up in San Diego with hundreds of layoffs at chipmaker
articles.summary: The cuts come weeks after CEO Cristiano Amon announced a "performance-focused reduction" following annual reviews.
articles.body:
One of the biggest smartphone chipmakers is laying off hundreds of workers across California.

San Diego-based Qualcomm is laying off 442 employees in San Diego and 75 employees at various locations in Santa Clara County, according to Worker Adjustment and Retraining Notifications filed last week.

The permanent layoffs will take effect by Jan. 12.

The cuts follow a memo Qualcomm Chief Executive Cristiano Amon sent to staff last month saying the company would carry out a "performance-focused reduction" after its annual employee reviews.

"As we have expanded the business, so have the competencies ⁠and skills we require," Amon said in the memo.

This is not the first round of cuts at Qualcomm this year. In April, the company filed notices eliminating 105 jobs in San Diego.

"These decisions are difficult because they affect our colleagues, and we're grateful for their contributions," a Qualcomm spokesperson said. "We are making these changes to ensure our organization and capabilities are aligned with our evolving priorities and the opportunities ahead. We are committed to supporting impacted employees with care and respect throughout the transition."

Founded in 1985 in San Diego, Qualcomm has grown to 170 offices across 30 countries and more than 50,000 employees.

Qualcomm designs chips and wireless technology for phones and other devices, and Apple and Samsung are among its largest customers. Apple and Samsung accounted for 10% or more of fiscal 2026 revenue.

The smartphone business is under pressure, with Qualcomm hit this year by a slump in consumer electronics sales and soaring memory prices.

Qualcomm acknowledged those strains in a filing to the Securities and Exchange Commission.

The company said it expects Apple to "primarily" use its own internally developed modems going forward. In a July earnings call, Qualcomm executives said Apple-related revenue would fall about 50% from the September quarter to the December quarter, and come in below $2 billion in fiscal 2027.

In its SEC filing, Qualcomm listed customers developing their own chips and its concentration in China, amid U.S.-China trade and national security tensions, among its risk factors.

Qualcomm reported its fourth-quarter results on Nov. 4. Revenue was $10.32 billion, down 8% from the prior year.

The company said it expects most of its 2027 chip sales to come from businesses other than smartphones.

Its shares, which have slid more than 20% in the last six months, were trading near $160 on Wednesday.

This story originally appeared in Los Angeles Times .

articles.title: Skydance's David Ellison calls Elon Musk 'the greatest entrepreneur of our time'
articles.summary: David Ellison, CEO of Skydance, expressed gratitude for Elon Musk's investment in the company.
articles.body:
Skydance's ( SKYD ) David Ellison said on Wednesday he thinks SpaceX ( SPCX ) and Tesla ( TSLA ) CEO Elon Musk is the "greatest entrepreneur of our time," but that a critical documentary about the billionaire will still appear on Ellison's streaming service.

The media magnate spoke at the New York Times' DealBook summit on Wednesday and discussed Musk's recent investment in Skydance. In October, Semafor reported that Musk invested $1 billion in Skydance, which Ellison confirmed.

"He doesn't invest in a lot of companies. So to have his vote of confidence and to have him as a shareholder is an honor and a privilege," Ellison said.

On whether it signaled a larger partnership, Ellison said he was "thrilled" to have him as a shareholder and that the door is open for more collaboration.

"I mean, he is both, you know, Tesla, Edison … he is the greatest entrepreneur of our time," Ellison said. "If there was any opportunity to be able to collaborate with him in the future, from our perspective, it would be a privilege."

Commentators and social media users had speculated that Musk's $1 billion investment was a quid pro quo to prevent Alex Gibney's documentary about Musk from streaming on HBO. However, Ellison dismissed those rumors, stating that Skydance and HBO had a pay-one deal with A24, which produced the film, and that the company would follow through with it.

"We believe in independence. We don't believe in censorship of any kind, and we have that deal with A24, and of course we'll honor it," Ellison said.

articles.title: Another AI company is about to be worth more than $1 trillion. What that means for the rest of us.
articles.summary: Leading AI lab Anthropic is expected to make the largest-ever public market debut when it starts trading on the Nasdaq stock exchange Thursday.
articles.body: Leading AI lab Anthropic is expected to make the largest-ever public market debut when it starts trading on the Nasdaq stock exchange Thursday. Founded in 2021 by brother and sister Dario and Daniela Amodei, both former employees of rival OpenAI, Anthropic and its main product, Claude, are seen as the gold standard of AI models, despite lacking the household-name cache of ChatGPT. With a target market value of $1.5 trillion — larger than SpaceX’s record setting IPO just a few months ago — Anthropic’s public arrival will serve as more than just a measure of what Wall Street thinks the company is worth. It will be a test of current sentiment around AI itself at a pivotal moment for the industry. For much of the past year, the AI investment wave has powered the stock market to new heights and sustained U.S. economic growth. But there are signs the wave may be starting to break. “Investors have over recent weeks become increasingly concerned around the sustainability of the investment boom,” James McCann, senior economist for investment strategy at Edward Jones, said in a client note Wednesday ahead of Anthropic’s debut. The market gains notched this spring and summer thanks to the AI boom have now largely been wiped out. Fears of over-spending on infrastructure, rising debt loads, ballooning costs and uncertain demand have grown. At the same time, public opinion has turned against data centers and AI-skeptical Democrats won control of Congress earlier this month. Then, the Jensen Huang scandal broke, creating a cloud of uncertainty over Nvidia, a company at the heart of the AI economy. The tech heavy Nasdaq was up 19% for the year recently. As of Wednesday, it’s higher by less than 5%. “The leadership change at Nvidia meanwhile adds to short-term uncertainty around the sector, particularly given the important role this giant company has played in financially supporting a range of smaller technology firms in recent years,” said McCann. “With the selloff in technology stocks continuing this week investors will be watching to see how well the Anthropic IPO is received.” The offering priced Anthropic at $83 a share, above the company’s intended range, the company said late Wednesday. There is little debate over how uniquely successful Anthropic has been. The latest edition of Claude, dubbed Fable, ranks No. 1 on Artificial Analysis’ leaderboard of top-performing large language models as it is able to handle complex computer engineering tasks. And its Claude Code application is now used throughout the tech industry and by some accounts became the fastest-growing product in enterprise software history when it was released in Feb. 2025, hitting $1 billion in revenues within six months of launching. Thursday’s IPO is also expected to mint a new crop of billionaires and multi-millionaires as Anthropic’s co-founders and early employees see their interest in the company turned into shares with a defined cash value. Part of that will be fueled by a massive appetite for investing in the shares among mom-and-pop investors. According to Vanda Research, a markets consultancy, Anthropic could see approximately $250 million worth of buying among non-institutional or “retail” investors when it starts trading Thursday. That would be double the magnitude of interest following SpaceX’s IPO. Other major winners will include Amazon, Google-parent Alphabet, Microsoft, and Nvidia, which will each own billions-worth of Anthropic shares. Some observers see Anthropic’s debut as more of a major milestone than a make-or-break moment. In their view, there are plenty of other investments backstopping the AI boom. “A strong IPO would help resurrect the AI trade, but it does not mean a weaker-than-expected IPO would bury that trade,” said Renée Friedman, global head of research at EXANTE, a Europe-based finance and technology group. “There are significant commitments into the AI cycle by some of the world’s largest companies over a multi-year period. These are not going to just disappear,” he said. In the first half of 2026, Anthropic saw total revenues of more than $16 billion. That compares with $41 million over the same period just three years ago. While Anthropic was technically operating at a loss to start the year, investors expect it to be profitable soon. Those heady figures capture a tension at the heart of Anthropic’s IPO. In addition to being the leading AI lab, current and former Anthropic employees have also been some of the most vocal proponents of AI safety, giving voice to fears that, should the technology become too advanced, it could start to run amok. “I think that without international coordination we will incur a risk of causing human extinction,” former Anthropic employee Jacob Coxon wrote of his concerns about AI shortly before resigning. Yet some critics have said those concerns have proven no match for the seemingly unstoppable momentum of creating a company publicly valued at more than $1 trillion. Dario Amodei has responded, arguing building safe AI and creating the world’s most advanced — and valuable — AI models are not necessarily mutually exclusive. When a user criticized Anthropic for seeming to plunge ahead with its attempt to create “superhuman” AI despite the risks to humanity doing so, Amodei replied in an X post that “a list of things that Anthropic did in the past year that were pro-safety and commercially costly to us” would be much longer than a list of risks it posed to mankind.

articles.title: US lawmakers push to raise minimum wage to $25, end tipped pay system
articles.summary: Public support for raising the minimum wage grows, with 78 percent of voters saying it was an important election issue.
articles.body:
In Washington, DC, a group of lawmakers has ramped up calls to increase the United States federal minimum wage and eliminate the subminimum wage, otherwise known as the tipped wage.

The group of 17 lawmakers, which includes current and newly elected House members, is calling for passage of the Living Wage For All Act, which has been languishing since it was introduced in April.

The legislation’s original lead sponsors include Representative Delia Ramirez of Illinois, Representative Jesus “Chuy” Garcia, also of Illinois, and Representative Analilia Mejia of New Jersey.

The bill aims to gradually raise the federal minimum wage to $25 an hour, with different timelines depending on the size of the employer.

Brad Lander, a congressman-elect from Brooklyn, New York, who says he will join the bill as a co-sponsor when the next congressional session begins in January, told Al Jazeera: “Doing it federally is the right way to go. Tying it into broader legislation that raises the minimum wage for all workers is a great approach.”

For larger employers — those with more than 500 employees nationwide or at least $1bn in annual revenue — the increase would be completed by 2031. Smaller employers would have until 2038.

After that, the minimum wage would be maintained at two-thirds of the US median hourly wage, with annual adjustments to preserve that ratio.

The bill would also eliminate the separate subminimum wage for tipped workers, currently $2.13 an hour. Under the existing framework, employers can count workers’ tips towards their minimum-wage requirements.

While several states have raised their own minimum wages, the federal rate remains $7.25 an hour, where it has stood since 2009. Washington, DC, has the highest minimum wage of any US jurisdiction, at $18.40 an hour, followed by Washington state at $17.13. However, 20 states do not have a minimum wage higher than the federal rate. Those states include Texas, Georgia and Iowa.

Laws governing the subminimum wage also vary across states. Seven states require employers to pay tipped workers the full minimum wage before tips, including Alaska, California and Nevada.

Others, including New York, have higher tipped cash wages than the federal rate but allow employers to take a tip credit, meaning they can pay workers less than the standard minimum wage as long as their tips make up the difference.

In New York, minimum wages vary by region. The rate is $17 an hour in New York City and its surrounding suburbs, and $16 an hour in the rest of the state.

For tipped workers outside the food service industry, the minimum cash wage is $14.15 in the New York City metropolitan area and $13.30 elsewhere in the state. For restaurant workers, those rates are $11.35 and $10.70, respectively.

The distinction is a point of contention for Lander.

“All workers deserve a raise. The 45 million working people who make less than $20 an hour deserve a raise, and the tipped subminimum wage is inexcusable at this point,” he said.

The subminimum wage has long been viewed as a legacy of racial and economic inequalities that disproportionately affected Black Americans. When Congress passed the Fair Labor Standards Act in 1938, establishing the first federal minimum wage, it excluded categories of workers in domestic and agricultural occupations, which disproportionately employed Black Americans.

Congress extended federal minimum-wage protections to restaurant and other service workers in 1966. But rather than requiring employers to pay tipped workers the full minimum wage, lawmakers established a separate tipped minimum wage, initially set at 50 percent of the standard federal rate. Employers could count customers’ tips towards the rest of a worker’s minimum-wage obligation. In 1996, Congress froze the federal tipped cash wage at $2.13 an hour, where it remains today.

The purchasing power of the standard federal minimum wage has also changed drastically. Adjusted for inflation, the $7.25 minimum wage in 2009 would be worth $11.32 today, meaning it has lost 36 percent of its purchasing power.

The federal minimum wage’s purchasing power peaked in 1968, when the rate was $1.60 an hour. Adjusted for inflation, that peak would be worth significantly more than the current minimum wage, representing a loss of roughly 53 percent in purchasing power.

The push to raise wages also has public support. A new poll released on Wednesday by One Fair Wage, an organisation that has long campaigned to eliminate the subminimum wage, found that 78 percent of voters considered raising the minimum wage to $25 an hour an important factor in their vote in the recent US midterm elections, where Republicans were dealt massive losses with the cost of living a key issue for voters.

“Washington has allowed the federal minimum wage to become increasingly disconnected from the economic reality facing American families,” Saru Jayaraman, president of One Fair Wage, said in a statement.

The push for the Living Wage For All Act comes as Democrats prepare to take control of both the House and Senate in the new Congress.

The last major attempt to raise the federal minimum wage came during former President Joe Biden’s first year in office. Democrats sought to increase the rate from $7.25 to $15 an hour through the Raise the Wage Act of 2021, which was included in the original proposal for Biden’s American Rescue Plan.

Ultimately, the effort failed after the Senate rejected a motion to waive budgetary rules that would have allowed the minimum-wage increase to proceed. The March 2021 vote was 42–58, with all Republicans opposed, joined by seven Democrats and independent Senator Angus King of Maine, who caucuses with Democrats.

Although the legislation failed, Biden raised the minimum wage for federal contract workers to $15 an hour in 2022 through an executive order. President Donald Trump revoked that order in 2025.

articles.body: New Delhi: Employees' Provident Fund Organisation is set to unveil a systematic withdrawal plan meant to allow voluntary contributions by gig and unorganised sector workers, while also giving crores of its existing subscribers the option to use the instrument since many are unable to invest their retirement corpus prudently. The proposal is scheduled to be discussed by the central board of trustees headed by labour minister Mansukh Mandaviya on Thursday.To begin with, the voluntary scheme is meant to focus on existing subscribers, with EPFO estimating that 6.3 lakh members who are above 55 years at present could be potential beneficiaries in the initial phase.Currently, they have to withdraw the entire corpus within three years of retirement, before their account turns inoperative, meaning it will stop earning annual interest. Instead, they will now be given the option to withdraw a part of the funds, which can be done periodically - monthly, quarterly or annually.The withdrawal period can extend up to a prescribed tenure and the funds will remain invested in EPF and continue to earn interest, people familiar with the proposal told TOI.Subscribers will also have the option to stop the SWP whenever they want to, apart from partial lump-sum withdrawal or only withdrawing the interest earned.EPFO to allow micro-contributions like tipsEPFO may soon give members the option to make voluntary contributions into their EPF account through digital means, with the employer not required to make any matching contribution. The contributions will, however, be in line with limits prescribed under Income Tax Act.The system is proposed to be opened up for gig and unorganised sector workers. EPFO will also allow micro-contributions, such as tips, gratuity and gifts through a universal account number-linked digital payment mechanism.The labour ministry has been looking to use EPF as a tool for long-term savings by gig and unorganised sector workers since the new Social Security Code was implemented, but Centre has to extend SWP to the sector so domestic workers, construction workers, street vendors and others are included under the umbrella.Those familiar with the with tax benefits available on investments and interest income up to Rs 2.5 lakh annually. articles.title: Moody’s Lowers Nvidia’s Ratings Outlook to Stable From Positive
articles.summary: Moody’s Ratings cut its outlook for Nvidia Corp.’s credit to stable from positive, citing the resignation of longtime Chief Executive Officer Jensen Huang an...
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- Moody's Ratings cut its outlook for Nvidia Corp.'s credit to stable from positive, citing the resignation of longtime Chief Executive Officer Jensen Huang and the company's "lack of a formal succession plan."

Huang's exit "has introduced uncertainty about the company's business strategy and financial policies," Moody's Ratings Senior Vice President Raj Joshi said. "It also could have repercussions for the growth strategy, which is supported by Nvidia's vast network of relationships across the AI ecosystem."

The world's largest chipmaker cut ties with Huang on Nov. 12 after revelations about his extramarital affairs spurred a widening scandal. Huang has admitted to a relationship with a woman that the US government has investigated for spying on behalf of China. Beijing has denied the espionage plot. Nvidia, which Huang ran for more than 30 years, is now actively recruiting for his replacement and has approached Arm Holdings Plc Chief Executive Officer Rene Haas as part of its hunt.

US government investigations tied to Huang's admitted affair may also "distract management" at Nvidia, said Joshi, who also cited the Commerce Department's move to increase scrutiny of remote access of cloud computing and how that might negatively affect the company's sales.

Moody's affirmed Nvidia's Aa1 senior unsecured rating — the second highest for Moody's — and Prime-1 short-term commercial paper program rating. The lower outlook means an upgrade is unlikely over the next 12 to 18 months, the agency said.

articles.title: Cook rebuffs hearing on alleged mortgage fraud
articles.summary: Presented by Bitget. {beacon} Business & Economy Business & Economy The Big Story Lisa Cook rebuffs hearing on alleged mortgage fraud Lisa Cook, a member of the Federal Reserve board of governors, will not attend an upcoming White House hearing on allegations she committed mortgage fraud, her attorney said in a letter to White House…
articles.body:
Lisa Cook rebuffs hearing on alleged mortgage fraud

Lisa Cook, a member of the Federal Reserve board of governors, will not attend an upcoming White House hearing on allegations she committed mortgage fraud, her attorney said in a letter to White House officials .

“Governor Cook has no legal obligation to participate in an unfair hearing — and indeed, has a duty to the Federal Reserve to decline to participate in any proceeding that would undermine the institution’s unique status and independence,” Abbe Lowell , Cook’s lawyer, wrote Monday to White House counsel Will Scharf.

President Trump has sought to fire Cook since the summer of 2025 over allegations she committed mortgage fraud. The Trump administration has alleged that Cook previously claimed two primary residences to receive better terms on loans, claims the Fed governor has denied.

The White House sought to have Cook appear before a three-member panel featuring Kevin Hassett , the director of the National Economic Council (NEC), Labor Secretary Keith Sonderling and Andrea Lucas , the chair of the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission.

Lowell’s letter, which copied the three committee members, specifically singled out Hassett as “not competent to serve on any factfinding committee” on the matter.

The NEC director, the letter stated, has “prejudged” the issue by previously saying Cook should resign amid the allegations.

“As evidenced by his past comments about Governor Cook , Mr. Hassett has ‘already prejudged the case,’ such ‘that the ultimate determination of the merits will move in predestined grooves,’” Lowell wrote, citing legal precedent.

The Supreme Court in June blocked Trump’s attempt to fire Cook for cause. Chief Justice John Roberts wrote at the time that the president did not give Cook enough process to contest the allegations.

Cook, whom former President Biden appointed to the Fed board in 2022, is a member of the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) — which sets monetary policy.

Trump has repeatedly urged the FOMC to cut interest rates. Former Fed Chair Jerome Powell , who still sits on the FOMC, even alleged the Justice Department’s since-scratched probe of central bank renovations was a pretext for pressuring officials to slash rates in line with the president’s preference.

Welcome to The Hill’s Business & Economy newsletter , I’m Max Rego — covering the intersection of Wall Street and Pennsylvania Avenue.

Capitol Hill lawmakers, travel industry experts and the head of the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) discussed how American aviation needs to evolve on Wednesday, less than a week after the first nationwide ground stop since January 2023.

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said Wednesday that President Trump is not worried about Ottawa’s deepening trade ties with China.

articles.title: Is the AI party over? Anthropic is about to find out.
articles.summary: Bring on the hotly anticipated Anthropic IPO. The tech bulls and bears are ready.
articles.body:
Thursday is supposed to be a celebration of AI.

Anthropic ( ANT ) is heading toward its long-awaited IPO at the Nasdaq , potentially giving Wall Street one of the biggest new pure-play AI investment stories in years.

Before you hit me up on X , Elon Musk-led SpaceX ( SPCX ) is not a pure-play AI company. It's an industrial company with a whole lot of AI bolted on.

But there's a problem amid all the Anthropic IPO hoopla.

The very stocks that fueled this AI boom are still under pressure. Just look at the sell-offs this week in top tech names like CoreWeave ( CRWV ), Salesforce ( CRM ), and even AMD ( AMD ).

Investors are questioning the AI spending, the valuations, the financing arrangements — and whether the returns will ever justify the billions being poured into this technology.

And the timing couldn't be more fascinating.

Truist chief market strategist Keith Lerner noted that tech valuations have fallen 42% over the past year. The sector has gone from outperforming the S&P 500 ( ^GSPC ) by 25% over six months to underperforming it by 6%. Bank of America's latest fund manager survey shows investors have cut tech exposure by the most since June 2006.

The question pre-Anthropic IPO: Is Wall Street finally getting too negative?

The AI build-out isn't disappearing, as we saw from Nvidia ( NVDA ) on Tuesday. Companies are still spending. The technology is still evolving. And as Lerner pointed out, previous tech pullbacks of more than 10% during this bull market were followed by an average rebound of 47%.

That doesn't guarantee a repeat. There are real risks — and this AI stock sell-off could get worse.

Anthropic's IPO arrives at a moment when investors are suddenly asking what could go wrong with AI.

Maybe it's time to ask the other question: What could go right?

Investing in Anthropic is like investing in a young Amazon ( AMZN ), "Shark Tank" star Kevin O'Leary told me on Sozzi Unleashed . Valid point.

Indeed, the biggest opportunity in tech may emerge when Wall Street least wants to own it.

That's the trade I'm watching. Well, that and the first few ticks in ticker symbol ANT!

articles.title: Trade deal to be signed after US ready with tariff structure
articles.summary: New Delhi: After months of negotiations, India on Wednesday said a trade deal with the US can only be signed after the tariff framework is ready and
articles.body: New Delhi: After months of negotiations, India on Wednesday said a trade deal with the US can only be signed after the tariff framework is ready and investigations under section 301 are concluded. This puts an end to all speculations over status of trade deal.India and the US have been in talks for a bilateral trade deal since Feb 2025 and had finalised the first tranche of the agreement, which imposed 18% additional tariffs on Indian exports, but had to put it on hold after the US Supreme Court struck down "reciprocal tariffs". Commerce secretary Rajesh Agrawal said that India is now waiting for the new tariff architecture to be put in place.Currently over 55 countries, including India, face additional tariffs of 10-12.5% on grounds of their purported failure to act against imports using forced labour. The tariffs came after a section 301 probe, with a second investigation on 15 countries, underway for creating structural overcapacity in certain industries, which is hurting US producers."There are certain 301 investigations underway, they will also be coming to the fore in the next few weeks... every country would like to have a deal that gives it certainty around all these investigations that are going on. You can't have a deal till you have uncertainty around multiple investigations. Those numbers and the actual deal will be signed and operationalised once these investigations are over and are reaching maturity," Agrawal said at a Ficci event.The comment provides much-needed clarity, amid repeated statements from both sides on the deal being ready. Agrawal said that the negotiations for the text and other aspects are near finalisation. There is, however, no clarity on when the findings of the second probe will be released, which will be followed by hearings by the US Trade Representatives and the announcement of tariffs. The entire process will take around 45 days from the time the report is released.Negotiators believe that once the tariffs are announced, the US administration will bilaterally negotiate duties. Agrawal also said govt is trying to conclude negotiations for some of the trade deals by the end of the year with some "good news" expected in Dec too, in what was seen as a reference to the talks with Canada.Money habits form by age 7. articles.title: Companies are cautious on leverage: JPMorgan
articles.summary: MUMBAI:JPMorgan is deepening its corporate-banking relationships in India, financing nearly half its investment-banking deals.
articles.body: MUMBAI:JPMorgan is deepening its corporate-banking relationships in India, financing nearly half its investment-banking deals. In an interview with TOI, Pranav Chawda, CEO, JPMorganChase Bank India, discusses how healthier corporate balance sheets and more sophisticated borrowers are reshaping financing choices. Excerpts:Do corporate earnings justify rising valuations?They do justify the market rally. Companies have delivered strong results over the past two quarters despite volatility in logistics, raw-material and foreign-exchange costs, with little reason to expect a sharp slowdown. Valuations are now reasonable, with price-to-earnings multiples easing. More importantly, multiples should be seen against India's intact growth story and corporates' ability to withstand shocks while continuing to grow.How are corporates choosing between debt and capital markets?Indian corporates remain cautious on leverage, preferring internal cash flows to fund modest capex amid strong earnings and free cash generation. They are borrowing selectively for transformative deals and large outbound acquisitions, often planning subsequent QIPs or equity raises to pare debt. Companies that borrowed over the past 12-18 months are also using elevated share prices to deleverage. Capital-market fundraising, particularly IPOs, is expected to remain strong, though debt-equity funding patterns will vary by sector and financial sponsors' exit timelines. Having said that, the debt cost or the amount that they can raise is still cheaper from an onshore perspective.Has rupee stabilised?The rupee is showing early signs of stabilisation, with RBI measures helping narrow the demand-supply gap by removing oil payments from the market. Importers have cut hedges, while exporters are reconsidering theirs, suggesting the measures are beginning to influence the behaviour RBI sought to change. However, softer West Asia tensions and lower oil prices have also helped, making the recent 2-3 weeks insufficient to establish a lasting trend.How is the demand for external commercial borrowing?The rise in ECB volumes largely reflects banks leveraging the RBI window (for subsidised forex hedging), not a surge in corporate capex funding. Corporates continue to find rupee loans cheaper as elevated hedging costs still make fully hedged ECBs 50-150 basis points costlier. ECB demand is concentrated in specific cases such as acquisitions, inter-group funding and time-sensitive or onshore-unfundable requirements. MNCs are willing to pay a 50-100 bps premium for such funding. Most eligible borrowers have already used the RBI window, ruling out a last-minute rush before its end-October expiry.Do you expect foreign portfolio flows to sustain?The sustainability of FII inflows hinges on channelling index-linked and other long-term foreign capital into long-gestation domestic assets, making flows stickier. Recent inflows driven by investors hedging the AI trade remain uncertain and depend on global AI investment trends, data-centre expansion and regulatory safeguards. The key indicators are whether announced AI capex translates into actual investment and projects ramp up as planned. A sustained rollout would signal a revival in the AI trade; delays could reverse the flows.What innovations have you brought in corporate financing?Our innovation lies in tailoring funding to each client's needs, whether episodic or recurring. An ECB may initially seem suitable, but a dollar loan, offshore borrowing or GIFT City structure may work better as a deal evolves. articles.title: Sebi studying various SLBM models: Pandey
articles.summary: Mumbai: Sebi chairman Tuhin Kanta Pandey on Wednesday said that the markets regulator was studying various models for stock lending-borrowing mechanism
articles.body: Mumbai: Sebi chairman Tuhin Kanta Pandey on Wednesday said that the markets regulator was studying various models for stock lending-borrowing mechanism (SLBM) from around the world to have a suitable system for the Indian market. He also ruled out extending trading hours, saying such a change would mean increased risks, liquidity issues etc. The Sebi chief said there was no decision taken by the regulator relating to margin trade finance (MTF) rules.Pandey was responding to reporters after addressing the 65th general assembly and annual meeting of the World Federation of Exchanges (WFE).During his address, Pandey also said that technology will continue to reshape market infrastructure. "Artificial intelligence and advanced analytics offer significant opportunities in market surveillance, risk monitoring, regulatory compliance and investor services. At the same time, AI introduces challenges relating to model reliability, data governance, cybersecurity and dependence on a limited number of technology providers. Hence, the objective should be to encourage innovation while ensuring that governance and safeguards keep pace," he said.The top regulator also said that many of the challenges that regulators around the world are facing currently are not confined to national boundaries. "Cyber threats, technological dependencies, market volatility and cross-border financial linkages affect exchanges and clearing corporations across jurisdictions. While our markets differ in size, structure and maturity, our underlying objectives remain similar: Fair and transparent markets, investor confidence and financial stability."Pandey said that these are the areas where organisations such as WFE play a valuable role. On the issue of extending trading hours in India, Pandey said it's not a priority for the regulator because that could increase cybersecurity risks, overnight volatility and also bring with it liquidity concerns.On the issue of SLBM, the Sebi chairman said that the regulator was in favour of transparent, exchange-based models for stock lending-borrowing mechanism.Money habits form by age 7. articles.title: Anthropic’s $83 IPO price puts it on track for a record-breaking debut on Wall Street. Here’s what it means
articles.summary: Anthropic said Wednesday it plans to sell shares in its initial public offering at an even higher price than expected, aiming for the largest stock market debut of all time.
articles.body: Anthropic said Wednesday it plans to sell shares in its initial public offering at an even higher price than expected, aiming for the largest stock market debut of all time. Anthropic confirmed the IPO will include a sale of 980 million shares at $83 a share, raising $81.3 billion — and surpassing SpaceX’s $75 billion IPO as the biggest on record. The IPO will be a major event for Wall Street, and a pivotal moment for the artificial intelligence boom that’s become a driving force behind the stock market. The final pricing comes after Anthropic spent the past few days pitching its public offering to different investors. Anthropic initially set a target range for its shares at $70 to $78 a share, but the new pricing above the original range signals strong investor demand. Anthropic also raised the total number of shares being sold, up from 825 million. Anthropic said in a statement late Wednesday that it would issue roughly 956 million shares, while “certain selling stockholders” would sell roughly 24 million shares, bringing the total number of shares to 980 million. Anthropic is set to start trading on the Nasdaq on Thursday under the ticker “ANT.” The strong IPO pricing comes despite recent market jitters. The tech-focused Nasdaq Composite has dropped more than 10% since its record high; and Nvidia, which has been a major component of the AI trade, is down 30% in the past month. Investors have been looking for signs of strength especially since the resignation of former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who left after admitting to an extramarital affair with potential national security implications. The IPO price is set by the company and the bankers underwriting the offering after gauging investors’ interest, and it’s what investors participating in the public offering will pay. But it’s not necessarily the price people will be paying when the stock hits the market. The opening price of the stock is determined based on the fundamentals of supply and demand. For example, SpaceX set its IPO price at $135 a share, and opened on the stock market at $150 a share. Once trading begins, the price will fluctuate. Investors at major institutions and financial firms often participate in IPOs, and they get first dibs on the shares. That’s not to say that retail investors who don’t work buying stocks for big companies will be left out in the cold. Companies can set aside shares for retail investors — or everyday people who trade or buy stocks in their own brokerage accounts — in IPOs. Anthropic is no different, and it’s set to put aside 20% of its offering for retail investors.

articles.title: 'India's challenge next year may be rupee's strength, not weakness': CEA Nageswaran
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: The country's challenge next year may be managing the rupee's strength rather than its weakness, chief economic advisor (CEA) V Anantha
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The country's challenge next year may be managing the rupee's strength rather than its weakness, chief economic advisor (CEA) V Anantha Nageswaran said on Wednesday, amid ongoing geopolitical uncertainties. His remarks come against the backdrop of volatility in the domestic currency, which has been appreciating in recent weeks.The rupee hit the lowest closing level of 96.88 against the US dollar on Oct 8, and since then it has rebounded, closing at 93.41 on Wednesday.Speaking at an event organised by Ficci, Nageswaran said India's exports have reached $568 billion in the first seven months of this fiscal, and are likely to touch the $1 trillion mark by March 2027."...look at the export numbers this year (fiscal) in the first seven months, $568 billion. Those of us who are not that mathematically challenged, we can easily extrapolate this to a 12-month number and say that we will be close to achieving a ($) trillion," Nageswaran said.India's total exports during April-Oct 2026-27 are estimated at $568.8 billion, up 16.7%. Total imports are estimated at $662.2 billion, a 16% rise year-on-year.Nageswaran further said, "We are approaching the end of the calendar year in a far better frame of mind than we would have found ourselves in six months ago". And if the prognosis of oil prices and what happens to the AI valuations is any indication, then 2027-28 could also turn out to be a fairly good year in terms of growth and capital flows to India." articles.title: EU governments approve trade deal with Indonesia to offset Trump tariffs
articles.summary: The deal, initially concluded in 2025, will see both sides remove import duties on more than 90 percent of products.
articles.body:
European Union governments have approved the signing of a previously agreed trade deal between the EU and Indonesia aimed at offsetting the impact of United States President Donald Trump’s tariffs .

The Council of the European Union’s decision on Wednesday also allows the deal to be applied provisionally. Both sides will remove import duties on more than 90 percent of products, and Indonesia’s 50 percent duty on EU cars will be eliminated within five years.

The deal will tie one of the world’s top economic blocs more closely to the fourth most populous country.

“These agreements will make it easier for European businesses to trade and invest, remove tariffs on almost all goods traded between the EU and Indonesia, and save businesses an estimated €600 million [$658.3m] annually in customs duties,” said Irish Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade Helen McEntee.

Indonesia has been negotiating a free trade and investment agreement with the EU since 2016. However, relations became strained after the European Commission decided to phase out palm oil from transport fuel by 2030 and imposed anti-subsidy duties on Indonesia’s biodiesel exports.

Both sides want the agreement, initially concluded in September 2025, to be applied as swiftly as possible. Indonesia will graduate from the EU’s generalised scheme of preferences on January 1, 2027, after which its exports will no longer benefit from preferential tariffs, the Council said in a statement.

The EU and Indonesia will now sign the agreements, which will then be submitted to the European Parliament for approval.
